entry.title: Not all Gradient Noise is Equal

link.title: Not all Gradient Noise is Equal

entry.content:
Intro

SGD never sees the exact gradient of the training loss. At every update, it computes a gradient from a randomly selected minibatch, and each minibatch gives a slightly different answer. The resulting optimization path is noisy rather than deterministic.

One common explanation is that this noise acts as an implicit regularizer. By continually perturbing the parameters, minibatch sampling may prevent SGD from remaining in sharp regions of the loss landscape and bias it toward flatter solutions that sometimes generalize better.

This story is not necessarily wrong, but it treats noise as though it were controlled by a single volume knob. In reality, noise has directions. Two noise distributions can have the same expected magnitude while pushing the parameters along completely different parts of the loss landscape. A perturbation along a high-curvature direction may change the loss substantially, while an equally large perturbation along a flat direction may do almost nothing.

To make this distinction precise, we need a model that describes both the geometry of the loss and the geometry of the noise. A useful starting point is the local quadratic model. The Hessian $H$ describes the curvature of the loss, while the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ describes how the noise variance is distributed across parameter directions. This model is simple enough to analyze exactly, yet rich enough to expose the interaction between curvature, noise magnitude, anisotropy, and alignment.

Following Zhu et al., we will see that this interaction is summarized locally by

\[\operatorname{tr}(H\Sigma)\]

We will eventually see that there is a connection between this analysis and the empirical observations of power-law eigenspectra in neural-network Hessians and stochastic-gradient covariance matrices and may have an impact on the generalization of real model training.

Preliminaries

We first setup our problem and give a brief review of some minibatch gradient properties.

Fix our dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Let $ heta$ be our model parameters, $\mathcal{L}( heta, \mathcal{D})$ be our empirical loss. We cond

Standard GD (gradient descent) typically involves optimizing:

\[\min_{ heta} \mathcal{L}( heta, \mathcal{D}) = \min_{ heta} rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(x_i; heta)\]

Where $x_i \in \mathcal{D}$ and for brevity $\ell(x_i, heta)$ is the loss associated with the observation $x_i$, incorporating the model’s computationi ($f_ heta(x_i)$ is left implicit).

Standard gradient descent does:

\[ egin{equation} heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta_t abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t) \end{equation}\]

However due to practical reasons, it is infeasible to calculate the gradient over the whole dataset of $N$ examples, hence stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is often used. Defining the unbiased estimator of the true gradient of the empirical loss $ abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta)$:

\[g( heta_t) := rac{1}{m} \sum_{x \in B_t} abla_ heta \ell(x; heta_t)\]

Here $B_t$ is a randomly selected minibatch of size $m$ selected uniformly from $\mathcal{D}$. The update rule for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is:

\[ egin{equation} heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta \hat{g}( heta_t) \label{eq:sgd-update} \end{equation}\]

Assuming that $m$ is large enough that the central limit theorem holds:

\[\hat{g}( heta_t) \sim \mathcal{N}( abla L( heta_t), \Sigma^{ ext{sgd}}( heta_t))\]

where

\[\Sigma^{ ext{sgd}}( heta_t) \approx rac{1}{m} \left[ rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N abla \ell(x_i; heta_t) abla \ell(x_i; heta_t)^ op - abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t) abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t)^ op ight]\]

Hence defining:

\[\varepsilon_t := \hat{g}(t) - abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma^{ ext{sgd}}( heta_t))\]

we may rewrite $\eqref{eq:sgd-update}$ as:

\[ heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t) + \eta \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma^{ ext{sgd}}( heta_t))\]

At this point, one can consider gradient Langevin dynamics, (GLD), where the update is of the form:

\[ heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t) + \eta \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2 I)\]

In fact GLD can be considered a discretization of the continuous time SDE taking the time between the discrete time steps to be $h := \eta$.

\[ egin{equation} d heta_t = - abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t) dt + \sqrt{\eta\Sigma_t} dW_t \label{eq:SDE-GLD} \end{equation}\]

Refer to the appendix for more details.

Minima Escaping Behavior

Consider the second order approximation of the loss:

\[ egin{equation} \mathcal{L}( heta) \approx \mathcal{L}( heta_0) + ( heta - heta_0) abla_ heta L( heta_0) + rac{1}{2} ( heta- heta_0)^ op abla^2_ heta L( heta_0) ( heta- heta_0) \end{equation}\]

Here we assume that $ heta_0$ is fixed and that $ heta_t$ is a random variable, as it depends on the noisy gradients.

Near a stationary point $ heta_0$, i.e.:

\[ abla_ heta L( heta_0) = 0\]

Near this stationary point, under the second-order approximation the loss is:

\[ egin{equation} \mathcal{L}( heta) \approx \mathcal{L}( heta_0) + rac{1}{2} ( heta- heta_0)^ op abla^2_ heta L( heta_0) ( heta- heta_0) \label{eq:stationary-second-order-approx} \end{equation}\]

That is the loss should be well approximated by a quadratic. In order to study generalization, we instead turn to a more tractable indicator and study how noise pushes the optimizer away from the minimum. Following the formulation of Zhu et al., define the escape efficiency:

\[ egin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{ heta_t}\left[ \mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) ight] \label{eq:escape-efficiency} \end{equation}\]

Again since $ heta_t$ is a random variable, we can consider the random variable:

\[ egin{equation} X := \mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) \end{equation}\]

If $ heta_0$ is a local minimum, then for sufficiently small $t$, by Markov’s inequality, for any $\delta > 0$:

\[ egin{equation} \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) \geq \delta) \leq rac{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0)]}{\delta} \end{equation}\]

The idea is that sharp minima attained during training may often generalize wrose than “flatter” solutioins. Here sharper means that smaller weight pertubataions in some directions may increase training loss substantially while a flatter solution, as its name implies is flat so small weight movement around this flatter minima, i.e. robustness to weight pertubations may (not always!) lead to accuracy on unseen examples.

Continuing, under sufficiently smooth assumptions, after applying Ito’s Lemma, $\eqref{eq:escape-efficiency}$ becomes:

\[\mathbb{E}_{ heta_t}\left[ \mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) ight] = - \int_0^t \mathbb{E}[ abla \mathcal{L}^ op abla L] + \int_0^t rac{1}{2} \mathbb{E} \operatorname{tr} (H_t \Sigma_t) dt\]

where $H_t := abla_ heta^2 \mathcal{L}( heta_t)$.

Under the assumption that $ heta_0$ is a local minimum (hence a stationary point), applying $\eqref{eq:stationary-second-order-approx}$ gives a tractable equation:

\[ egin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{ heta_t}[\mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0)] = rac{1}{4} \operatorname{tr}\left((I - e^{-2Ht})\Sigma ight) \label{eq:tractable-escape-efficiency} \end{equation}\]

For small $t$, $\eqref{eq:tractable-escape-efficiency}$ gives:

\[\operatorname{tr}\left((I - e^{-2Ht})\Sigma ight) \approx rac{t}{2} \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)\]

However as $t o \infty$ we instead have:

\[\operatorname{tr}\left((I - e^{-2Ht})\Sigma ight) \approx rac{1}{4} \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)\]

Hence there are two different regimes for how we want to measure escape efficiency. Note here $t$ is for the continuuous time representation of our discrete problem! That is for constant learning rate $\eta$, the next iteration of GLD is at the timestep:

\[t_{i+1} = t_i + \eta\]

Keep this in mind when intepreting the graphs and the experiments as adjusting the learning rate can change the regime we are operating in and which approximation holds.

Interpreting the Noise

Before continuing, the whole goal is to understand how the structure of noise introduced from SGD impacts generalization. Hence the effect of noise magnitude must be eliminated to create a fairer comparison. One reasonable metric for the noise magnitude is the expected square norm of the noise vector. Consider $QDQ^ op = \Sigma \succeq 0$. Let $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. Then define $\varepsilon := QD^{1/2} z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$. Therefore:

\[ egin{gather*} \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[\|\varepsilon\|_2^2]= \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon} [\varepsilon^ op \varepsilon] = \mathbb{E}_{z}[z^ op D^{1/2} Q^ op Q D^{1/2} z] \ = \mathbb{E}_{z}[\operatorname{tr}(z^ op D z)] = \mathbb{E}_{z}[\operatorname{tr}(D z^ op z)] = \operatorname{tr}(D) = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) \end{gather*}\]

Therefore given time $t$, $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_t)$ should be constant. That is we impose the constraint:

\[ egin{equation} \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) = c, \qquad c > 0 \label{eq:sigma-constraint} \end{equation}\]

However, the structure of $\Sigma_t$ and the induced curvature from $\Sigma_t$ may change. For example, consider $\Sigma_t \in \mathbb{R}^{2 imes 2}$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_t) = 1$. Then these two matrices satisfy the magnitude constraint, however lead to very different dynamics (as will be seen later):

\[\Sigma_1 = egin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma_2 = egin{bmatrix} 0.99999 & 0 \ 0 & 10^{-5} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma_3 = egin{bmatrix} 10^{-5} & 0 \ 0 & 0.99999 \end{bmatrix}\]

There is an intuitive interpretation for these “noise” matrices. For a fixed Hessian $H \in \mathbb{R}^{2 imes 2}$, say:

\[H = egin{bmatrix} 100 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

There is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors for $H$, particularly, $e_1, e_2$, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 100, \lambda_2 = 1$. Computing $\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)$ for each fo the noise matrices:

\[\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma_1) = 50.5, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma_2) = 99.99901, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma_3) = 1.00099\]

and recall that $\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)$ is directly tied to the escape effieciency, it is clear that the structure of noise could have an impact for escaping stationary points.

Generalizing the example further, suppose that $H \in \mathbb{R}^{D imes D}$ and $H \succeq 0$. So the eigen decomposition of $H = Q D Q^ op$ and the columns of $Q$ is an orthornomal basis of eigenvectors, say $q_1, \ldots, q_D$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_D$. Let $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}^D$ be a noise vector. Since $q_1, \ldots, q_D$ is an orthornomal basis of eigenvectors for $\mathbb{R}^D$, $\exists c_1, \ldots, c_D \in \mathbb{R}^D$ such that:

\[\varepsilon = \sum_{i=1}^D c_i q_i\]

In fact since $q_1, \ldots, q_D$ are orthonormal we have $ orall j$:

\[q_j^ op \varepsilon = c_i\]

Assuming $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$, we can consider the variances of each component of $\varepsilon$ in the direction of $q_j$:

\[ egin{align} \operatorname{Var}(c_j) = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[c_j^2] &= \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[(q_j^ op \varepsilon) (q_j^ op \varepsilon)^ op] otag \ &= q_j^ op \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[\varepsilon \varepsilon^ op ] q_j otag \ &= q_j^ op \Sigma q_j \label{eq:variance-in-direction} \end{align}\]

That is $q_j^ op \Sigma q_j$ can be interpreted as the variance of $\varepsilon$ in the direction of $q_j$.

This allows us to decompose $\operatorname{tr}(H\Sigma)$. To see why:

\[ egin{align*} \operatorname{tr}(H\Sigma) &= \operatorname{tr}\left(\sum_{i=1}^D \lambda_i q_i q_i^ op \Sigma ight) \ &= \sum_{i=1}^D \lambda_i \operatorname{tr}\left(q_i q_i^ op \Sigma ight) \ &= \sum_{i=1}^D \lambda_i q_i^ op \Sigma q_i \ &= \sum_{i=1}^D \lambda_i \operatorname{Var}(c_i) \end{align*}\]

This precisely measures the total variance of $\varepsilon$ weighted by the eigenvalues of $H$. Intuitively, this means the more larger curvature directions with the noise having high variance in that direction, the more we can expect to escape local minima.

Going one step further, since $\Sigma \succeq 0$, we have an eigendecomposition of $\Sigma = U D_\Sigma U^ op$ where say the eigenvalues are $s_1, \ldots, s_D$ with eigenvectors $u_1, \ldots, u_D$, the columns of $U$. Then rewriting $\eqref{eq:variance-in-direction}$:

\[ egin{align} \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma H) &= \operatorname{tr}(\sum_{i, j} \lambda_i s_j q_i q_i^ op u_i u_i^ op) otag \ &= \sum_{i, j} \lambda_i s_j \operatorname{tr}(q_i^ op u_i (q_i^ op u_i)) & ext{ cylic property of trace} otag \ &= \sum_{i, j} \lambda_i s_j (q_i^ op u_j)^2 \label{eq:escape-efficiency-alignment} \end{align}\]

As it can be oberserved, it does not suffice for the eigenvalues alone of $\Sigma$ and $H$ to be similar. We also need that the eigenvectors of $\Sigma$ and $H$ to be pointing in the same direction, otherwise the term $q_i^ op u_j = 0$ when they are perpendicular. This will become important in the experimental section when testing on real networks as even if the eigenvalues of the Hessian and eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the noise follow a power law, misalignment in their directions may still lead to a low value of $\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)$.

Extreme Cases

Okay, so now that we have a better picture of what part of SGD makes it so that it can escape local minima, we wouuld like to have a baseline comparison. Consider the isotropic minima. That is $H= \lambda I$. Then $\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma) = \lambda \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$ which is invariant under our constraint.

How about when $\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)$ achieves the maximal value? For a fixed $H$ what should $\Sigma$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) = c$ for some $c > 0$ look like in this case? That is we want to solve:

\[\underset{\Sigma \succeq 0, \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)= c}{\max}\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma)\]

In fact taking the eigendecomposition of $H = QDQ^ op$ and where $D$ contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_D$, we claim that $\Sigma^* := c q_1 q_1^ op$ indeed attains the maximum.

To see this, consider any $\Sigma \succeq 0$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) =c$. Then:

\[ egin{align*} \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma) &= \sum_{i=1}^D \underbrace{\geq 0}_{\lambda_i q_i^ op \Sigma q_i} \ &\leq \sum_{i=1}^D \lambda_1 q_i^ op \Sigma q_i \ &= \lambda_1 \sum_{i=1}^D \operatorname{tr}(q_i^ op \Sigma q_i) \ &= \lambda_1 \operatorname{tr}(\sum_{i=1}^D q_i q_i^ op \Sigma) \ &= \lambda_1 \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) \ &= \lambda_1 c \end{align*}\]

Note that $\operatorname{tr}(c q_1 q_1^ op) = c \operatorname{tr}(q_1^ op q) = c$. Also:

\[ egin{align*} \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma^*) &= \sum_{i=1}^D \lambda_i c q_i^ op q_1 q_1^ op q_i \ &= \lambda_1 c \end{align*}\]

In the context of $\eqref{eq:escape-efficiency-alignment}$, $H = c q_1 q_1^ op$ is perfectly aligned with $H$ in the direction of $q_1$, with all of its variance being pushed in the direction $q_1$, which allows for faster escape from a stationary point.

Experiments

We can transform the $\eqref{eq:escape-efficiency}$ into a quadratic problem centered at $ heta_0$. See the Appendix for more details. Originally we have:

\[\mathcal{E}_k := \mathbb{E}_{ heta_k \sim P_k} [L( heta_k) - L( heta_0)]\]

Consider the displacement from $ heta_0$ as:

\[ egin{equation} \delta_k := heta_k - heta_0 \label{eq:update-rule-delta} \end{equation}\]

Define:

\[ egin{equation} F(d) := \mathcal{L}( heta_0 + d) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) = rac{1}{2} d^ op H d \end{equation}\]

Then assuming the second order approximation and stationary point, we can consider the equivalent problem:

\[F(\delta) = rac{1}{2} ( heta- heta_0)^ op abla_ heta^2 L( heta_0) ( heta - heta_0) = rac{1}{2} \delta^ op abla_theta^2 \mathcal{L}( heta_0) \delta\]

Defining $H := abla_ heta^2 \mathcal{L}( heta_0)$, we would like to see observe the effects of different structure of noise and Hessians on the training dynamics of GLD near this stationary point $ heta_0$. And ideally, give an approximation of how the relationship between the noise in training and the Hessian of the true empirical loss function affect average escape from minima.

Constant Learning Rate, Hessian and Noise Structure

Consider the most basic case. A constant learning rate $\eta$, constant hessian $H$ and constant $\Sigma^{ ext{sgd}}$ where $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma^{ ext{sgd}})$. It has been observed that Hessians of neural networks, particularly CNNs and LLMs follow some sort of power law. This motivates us to test spectral distributions for $H$, $\Sigma$ that follows a power law. Additional spectral distributions were added as well for comparison.

Additionally, as GLD is standard GD with added noise, a stable learning rate is chosen so that the observed loss growth is caused by the injected noise and its intercation with the curvature of $H$, rahter than the instability of the numerical update.

Following the update rule induced by $\eqref{eq:update-rule-delta}$, we use the following update rule:

\[\delta_{k+1} = \delta_k - \eta abla F(\delta_k) + \eta \varepsilon_k, \quad \varepsilon_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_k)\]

Since $\delta_0 = 0$, we have for the first step:

\[\delta_1 = \delta_0 - \eta H \delta_0 + \eta \varepsilon_0 = \eta \varepsilon_0\]

Hence:

\[ egin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\delta_1}[F(\delta_1) - F(\delta_0)] = \mathbb{E}_{\delta_1}[F(\delta_1)] &= \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[F(\eta \varepsilon_0)] otag \ &= \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[ rac{1}{2}(\eta \varepsilon_0)^ op H (\eta \varepsilon_0)] otag \ &= rac{\eta^2}{2} \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[\varepsilon_0^ op H \varepsilon_0] otag \ &= rac{\eta^2}{2} \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[\operatorname{tr}(\varepsilon_0^ op H \varepsilon_0)] otag \ &= rac{\eta^2}{2} \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[\operatorname{tr}( H \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_0^ op)] otag \ &= rac{\eta^2}{2} \operatorname{tr}(H \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_0^ op]) otag \ &= rac{\eta^2}{2} \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma) \end{align}\]

So in fact the very first update is impacted by the escape efficiency. And in turn we can characterize the escape efficiency in terms of the expected loss from the first update. That is:

\[ egin{equation} rac{2}{\eta^2} \mathbb{E}_{\delta_1}[F(\delta_1)] = \operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma) \end{equation}\]

To isolate the effect of noise structure, we enforce the constraint from $\eqref{eq:sigma-constraint}$. Further for simplicity, we assume that both $H$ and $\Sigma$ are diagonal, so then the orthonormal eigenvectors is just the standard basis for both. To highlight the importance of alignment between the noise covariance and hessian, we introduce an aligned and reversed configuration. For the aligned configuration, the assigned diagonal index of the larger eigenvalues coincide with the large Hessian eigenvalues. For the reversed assignment, the same noise eigenvalues are assigned in opposite order. I.e.:

\[\Sigma_{ ext{aligned}} = egin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ 0 & \cdots & \lambda_D \end{bmatrix} \qquad \Sigma_{ ext{reversed}} = egin{bmatrix} \lambda_D & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ 0 & \cdots & \lambda_1 \end{bmatrix}\]

As can be seen in Figure 1 depends strongly on the pairing between curvature of the Hessian and noise variance. We can see that for the reversed alignment, the expected escape efficiency is very low, highlighting the fact that the $(u_i^ op q_i)^2$ term which measures alignment, really does matter.

For the one-small spectra distribution, it makes sense that many of the reversed assignments work well. This is because most of the eigenvalues of the Hessian are the same (and are large), hence any assignment that places little of the total curvature in the first direction will still result in a high escape efficiency. I.e. for one-small spectra distribution, the hessian is:

\[H = ext{diag}(h_{max}, \ldots, h_{max}, h_{min})\]

So:

\[\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma_{reversed}) = h_{max} \sum_{i=2}^D s_i + h_{min} s_1 = h_{max}(1-s_1) + h_{min} s_1\]

assuming that $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) = 1$.

If $h_{min} \ll h_{min}$, then:

\[\operatorname{tr}(H \Sigma_{reversed}) = h_{max}(1-s_1) + h_{min s_1} \approx h_{max}(1-s_1)\]

When Alignment Matters

Previously we showed that alignment is crucial for escape efficiency. However there are actually cases when it does not matter! Consider the two dimensional cases:

\[H_\kappa= egin{bmatrix} \kappa&0\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad S= egin{bmatrix} ho&0\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Define:

\[\Sigma_{\mathrm{aligned}} = egin{bmatrix} ho&0\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma_{\mathrm{reversed}} = egin{bmatrix} 1&0\ 0& ho \end{bmatrix}\]

Then

\[\operatorname{tr}(H_\kappa\Sigma_{\mathrm{aligned}})=\kappa ho+1, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(H_\kappa\Sigma_{\mathrm{reversed}})=\kappa + ho\]

Hence their ratio is:

\[ rac{\kappa ho+1}{\kappa+ ho}.\]

This gives a a pretty clean explanation:

  • If \(\kappa = 1\): The Hessian is isotropic and the orientation of the noise does not matter.
  • If \( ho = 1\): The noise is isotropic and the orientation of the noise does not matter.
  • If both $H$ and $\Sigma$ are strongly anisotropic, then alignment matters substantially.

However as stated before, empirical results show that in practical training $H$ and $\Sigma$ indeed are highly anisotropic.

CNN Experiements

In practice, we are not using a constant laerning rate, the Hessian is not constant and the noise may not necessarily be drawn repeatedly from the same type of Gaussian. However assuming the genereal structure remains the same, we see if we can apply the results obtained on quadratics to CNNs.

In the following we train on Fahsion-MNIST and first try to reproduce some key results

Unfortunately, we do not obtain the exact same long term improvement claimed by the paper across multiple seeds. For short term durations however, we do indeed see similarities with the paper. Below we present the results.

Additionally we consider the power scaling run and add noise whose covariance matrix has a spectral distribution based upon the power law:

\[\lambda_k = C s^{-k}\]

for some constants $C, s > 0$ and where $k$ is the index of the diagonal of the covariance of the noise.

The fixed trace uses the SGD noise trace at at the GD-3000 checkpoint. It does not update the magnitude of the covariance of the noise and is most faithful in the sense to our quadratic tests. Dynamic trace estimates the expected sqaure magnitude of the noise to match the noise magnitude of SGD.

The dynamic Hessian recomputes the Hessian recomputes the Hessian $H_t = abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t)$ over the whole training dataset, so there is no noise from mini-batch estimation. The frozen Hessian uses the Hessian of the model at the GD-3000 checkpoint. The results show that both the structure of the noise and magnitude of the noise matter.

Conclusion

I began with a simple question: What effect does the noise in SGD have on training, and which properties of that noise produce the effect? The answer is more complicated than saying that more noise is better. We began by expressing minibatch SGD as full-batch gradient descent with an additional zero-mean noise term. Near a stationary point, a quadratic approximation of the loss then gave us a precise measure of the initial response to this noise:

\[\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon_0}[F(\delta_1)] = rac{\eta^2}{2}\operatorname{tr}(H\Sigma).\]

Here, \(H\) describes the local curvature of the loss and \(\Sigma\) describes the covariance of the noise. Decomposing this trace gives

\[\operatorname{tr}(H\Sigma) = \sum_{i,j}\lambda_i s_j(q_i^ op u_j)^2.\]

The eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ and $s_j$ tell us how the curvature and noise variance are distributed, while $(q_i^ op u_j)^2$ measures the alignment between their directions. Consequently, two noise distributions with the same total variance and even the same eigenvalues can interact with the loss landscape very differently.

The quadratic experiments illustrate this distinction directly. Under a fixed noise trace, placing more variance in high-curvature directions produces a larger initial expected loss increase. Reversing the same noise spectrum can greatly reduce this effect. Alignment becomes irrelevant when either the Hessian or the noise covariance is isotropic, since there is then no preferred direction with which to align.

The Fashion-MNIST experiments suggest that these ideas remain relevant outside the exact quadratic setting. Structured GLD noise based on Hessian or gradient-covariance information could outperform isotropic noise and continued full-batch gradient descent in our runs. In the power-law experiments, the best-performing configuration used dynamically refreshed Hessian directions, a dynamically adjusted noise magnitude, and an aligned spectrum. This suggests that the structure, orientation, and magnitude of the noise can all matter during training.

A further practical limitation is the cost of measuring curvature in modern neural networks. The assumption that useful information is contained in the Hessian spectrum is not new, but computing its leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors becomes increasingly difficult as model size grows. Recent work is beginning to develop methods for studying Hessian structure at the scale of models with tens of billions of parameters. Such methods may eventually make it possible to test whether the relationships studied here persist at a much larger scale.

Future Directions

Several questions remain open. One is whether the relationship between curvature, noise structure, and alignment persists during the fine-tuning of pretrained models. With methods such as LoRA, only a low-dimensional parameter subspace is trainable, so the relevant quantities may be the Hessian and noise covariance projected into that subspace.

Another direction is extending the analysis to AdamW. If $P_t$ denotes its time-dependent preconditioner, then the effective noise covariance is approximately

\[\Sigma_t^{\mathrm{effective}} = P_t\Sigma_tP_t^ op.\]

The relevant alignment may therefore involve the preconditioned loss geometry rather than the raw Hessian and noise covariance. Momentum also accumulates a weighted history of gradient noise:

\[\varepsilon_t+ eta\varepsilon_{t-1} + eta^2\varepsilon_{t-2}+\cdots.\]

Pan et al. analyze convergence of stochastic heavy-ball momentum under anisotropic noise on quadratic objectives. However, it remains unclear how momentum transforms time-varying or correlated noise in neural networks and whether the resulting alignment affects generalization. Studying these effects during large-scale training and fine-tuning would bring the analysis closer to modern optimization practice.

Appendix

In the proofs below, we assume the following:

  • The training dataset $\mathcal{D} := {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N$
  • Our model parameters $ heta$
  • $B_t$ is a uniformly sampled subset of size $m$:
\[\mathbb{P}(B_t = b) := rac{1}{ inom{N}{m}}, \qquad b \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N \}, \; |B| = m\]
  • Our per example loss, empirical losses and mini-batch losses are:
\[\ell_i( heta) := \ell(f_ heta(x_i), y_i) \qquad \mathcal{L}( heta) := rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i( heta) \qquad \widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{B_t}( heta) := rac{1}{m} \sum_{i \in B_t} \ell_i( heta)\]

where $f_ heta(x_i)$ is our model prediction

  • Gradient & Mini Batch Gradients:
\[g_i := abla_ heta \ell_i( heta), \qquad g := abla_ heta L( heta) = rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i \qquad \hat{g} := rac{1}{m} \sum_{i \in B} abla_ heta \ell_i( heta)\]

We indeed have that $\hat{g}$ is an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the empirical loss:

\[ egin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{B_t}[ \hat{g}] &= \mathbb{E}_{B_t} \left[ rac{1}{m} \sum_{i \in B} abla_ heta \ell_i( heta) ight] \ &= \mathbb{E}_{B_t} \left[ rac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^N {\mathbf{1}}_{i \in B_t} g_i ight] \ &= rac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{P}(i \in B_t) g_i \ &= rac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^N rac{ inom{N-1}{m-1}}{ inom{N}{m}} g_i \ &= rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i = g \end{align*}\]
  • Define the noise as:
\[\varepsilon := g - \hat{g} = - rac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^N {\mathbf{1}}_{i \in B_t} \left(g_i - g ight)\]

We make no assumptions about the distribution of the noise. Note however that:

\[\mathbb{E}_{B_t}[\varepsilon] = 0\]

Covariance of Mini-Batch Noise

To find:

\[\operatorname{Cov}_{B_t}(\hat{g}( heta_t))\]

by central limit theorem $\hat{g}( heta_t) \sim \mathcal{N}(g, \Sigma^{ ext{sgd}})$. Define

\[\varepsilon := g - \hat{g}_t\] \[ egin{align*} \Sigma^{ ext{sgd}} := \operatorname{Cov}_{B_t}(\hat{g}( heta_t))& = \mathbb{E}_{B_t} \left[(\hat{g}( heta_t) - abla_ heta L( heta) )(\hat{g}( heta_t) - abla_ heta L( heta))^ op ight] \ &= \mathbb{E}_{B_t} \left[(\varepsilon)(\varepsilon)^ op ight] \end{align*}\]

Define:

\[C := rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (g_i -g)(g_i-g)^ op\]

Note some additional properties to be used are:

\[\sum_{i=1}^N (g_i -g) = Ng - \sum_{i=1}^N = g_i\] \[ egin{align*} 0 &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^N (g_i - g) ight)\left(\sum_{j=1}^N (g_j - g)^ op ight) \ &= \sum_{i, j} (g_i -g)(g_j-g)^ op \ &= \sum_i (g_i -g)(g_i-g)^ op + \sum_{i eq j} (g_i -g)(g_j- g)^ op \end{align*}\]

Hence:

\[\sum_{i eq j} (g_i -g)(g_j-g)^ op = -\sum_{i=1}^N (g_i -g)(g_i-g)^ op = -NC ag{2}\]

Also:

\[ egin{align*} C &= rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (g_i -g)(g_i-g)^ op \ &= rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i g_i^ op - \left( rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i ight)g^ op - g\left( rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i ight)^ op + g g^ op \ &= rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i g_i^ op - gg^ op - gg^ op + gg^ op \ &= rac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N g_i g_i^ op - g g^ op ag{3} \end{align*}\]

Computation of $\varepsilon \varepsilon^ op$:

\[ egin{align*} \varepsilon \varepsilon^ op &= rac{1}{m^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N {\mathbf{1}}_{i \in B_t} {\mathbf{1}}_{j \in B_t} (g_i - g)(g_j - g)^ op \ \end{align*}\]

Hence:

\[ egin{align*} ext{Cov}_{B_t}(\varepsilon \varepsilon^ op) &= \mathbb{E}_{B_t}(\varepsilon \varepsilon^ op) \ &= rac{1}{m^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N \mathbb{E}_{B_t} \left[ {\mathbf{1}}_{i \in B_t} {\mathbf{1}}_{j \in B_t} ight] (g_i - g)(g_j - g)^ op \ &= rac{1}{m^2} \left[\sum_i \underbrace{\mathbb{P}(i \in B_t)}_{ rac{m}{N}} (g_i - g)(g_i - g)^ op + \sum_{i eq j} \underbrace{\mathbb{P}(i ,j \in B_t)}_{ rac{m(m-1)}{N(N-1)}} (g_i -g)(g_j-g)^ op ight] \ &= rac{1}{m^2} \left[mC - rac{m(m-1)}{N(N-1)} (NC) ight] \ &= rac{C}{m}\left( 1 - rac{m-1}{N-1} ight) \ &= rac{N-m}{m(N-1)} C \end{align*}\]

Therefore:

\[\operatorname{Cov}_{B_t}(\epsilon_{B_t}) = rac{N-m}{m(N-1)} \left[ rac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N} abla_ heta\ell_i( heta) abla_ heta\ell_i( heta)^ op - abla_ heta L( heta) abla_ heta L( heta)^ op ight]\]

When the size of the mini batch is small compared to the total size of the dataset, then:

\[ rac{N-m}{N-1} = 1 - rac{m-1}{N-1} \approx 1\]

Time Discretization of SDE

In this section, we show that GLD is a time discritization of the following SDE with constant timestep difference $h = \eta$.

\[d heta_t = - abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t) dt + \sqrt{\eta \Sigma_t} dW_t\]

Consider $h > 0$ (numerical time step size) and consider:

\[t_k = kh, \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\]

Note $W_t \in \mathbb{R}^D$ is a standard Brownian motion so it satisfies, $ orall b > a$:

\[W_b - W_a \sim \mathcal{N}(0, (b-a) I_D)\]

Defining:

\[ egin{gather*} \Delta W_k := W_{t_{k+1}} - W_{t_k} \mathcal{N}(0, h I_D) \ \Delta W_k = \sqrt{h} z_k, \qquad z_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_D) \end{gather*}\]

We can just use Euler-Maruyama approximation and obtain:

\[ heta_{k+1} = heta_k - h abla L( heta_k) + \sqrt{\eta h} \Sigma( heta_k)^{1/2} z_k\]

Taking $h = \eta$ and using the fact that:

\[\varepsilon_k = \Sigma( heta_k)^{1/2} z_k\]

and we obtain the GLD update rule and this shows that GLD is the discretizaton of $\eqref{eq:SDE-GLD}$ with $h = \eta$.

Transformation of Variables

We want to that translating the probelm preserves the noisy gradient dynamics and expected loss increases. So fix $ heta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and let $\eta > 0$. Define:

\[F: \mathbb{R}^D o \mathbb{R}, \quad F(d) := \mathcal{L}( heta_0 + d) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0)\]

Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ be a probability space and $(\varepsilon_k)_{k \geq 0}$ be random vectors on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$. We consider two updates:

\[ egin{align*} heta_0 &= heta_0, & heta_{k+1} &= heta_k - \eta abla \mathcal{L}( heta_k) + \eta \varepsilon_k \ \delta_0 &= 0, &\delta_{k+1} &= \delta_k - \eta abla F(\delta_k) + \eta \varepsilon_k \end{align*}\]

For every $k \geq 0$ we have:

\[\delta_k = heta_k - heta_0 ag{1}\]

Hence:

\[ orall k \geq 0, \; orall \omega \in \Omega, \; F(\delta_k(\omega)) = \mathcal{L}( heta_k(\omega)) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0)\]

Furthermore writing:

\[P_k := \mathbb{P} \circ heta_k^{-1} \qquad Q_k := \mathbb{P} \circ \delta_k^{-1}\]

we have that the escape efficiency for both parameters are the same. That is:

\[\mathbb{E}_{\delta_k \sim Q_k} [F(\delta_k)] = \mathbb{E}_{ heta_k \sim P_k}[\mathcal{L}( heta_k) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0)]\]

Hence it suffices to consider the dynamics on $\delta_k$ and the quadratic centered at $0$.

Proof: First by chain rule, it is clear that

\[ abla F (d) = abla \mathcal{L}( heta_0 + d)\]

We can show (1) by induction on $k$.

$k = 0$: True

$k \geq 0$: Let $\omega \in \Omega$. We have:

\[ egin{align*} \delta_{k+1}(\omega) &= \delta_{k}(\omega) - \eta abla F(\delta_k(\omega)) + \eta \varepsilon_k \ &= heta_{k}(\omega) - heta_0 - \eta abla \mathcal{L}( heta_k(\omega)) + \eta \varepsilon_k \ &= heta_{k+1}(\omega) - heta_0 \end{align*}\]

To see the expectations are equal, this is a standard pushforward measure argument. First define:

\[ egin{gather*} g: \mathbb{R}^D o \mathbb{R} \ g( heta) = \mathcal{L}( heta) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) \end{gather*}\]

Hence $g( heta_k) = \mathcal{L}( heta_k)- \mathcal{L}( heta_0)$.

We have:

\[ egin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\delta_k \sim Q_k} [F(\delta_k)] &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} F dQ_k \ &= \int_\Omega (F \circ \delta_k) d \mathbb{P} & ext{pushforward measure theorem} \ &= \int_\Omega (g \circ heta_k) d \mathbb{P} & F \circ \delta_k = g \circ heta_k \ &= \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} g d P_k \ &= \mathbb{E}_{ heta_k \sim P_k}\left[\mathcal{L}( heta_k) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) ight] \end{align*}\]
